planting.note: Install a deep polypropylene or HDPE rhizome barrier before planting; this running species spreads readily, especially in the damp, boggy sites where it thrives.

directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in consistently moist to wet, fertile soil; this species tolerates seasonal flooding and pond margins better than most Phyllostachys. Because it runs aggressively underground, always install a barrier at least 24 inches deep sunk into the soil around the planting area, or confine plantings to an island bed. Culms are slender and slightly zigzagged near the base, forming an airy grove useful for stabilizing wet banks. Provide full sun for the densest culm production, though it will tolerate light shade with a more open habit.

planting.note: Requires a deep rhizome barrier (18-24 inches) at planting time; this large running timber bamboo spreads vigorously once established and is considered invasive outside containment in warm-temperate climates.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in deep, fertile, well-drained soil and water regularly through the first two seasons while the grove establishes. The straight species carries solid golden-yellow culms (distinct from the green-culmed variety sold as Phyllostachys viridis), which color best with full sun exposure. Because it is a vigorous runner capable of colonizing large areas, install a sunken rhizome barrier before planting and inspect the perimeter annually for escaped shoots. Once established it forms a tall, stately timber grove suitable for large properties or screening.

planting.note: Install a sunken rhizome barrier (18+ inches deep) before planting; this is a vigorous cold-hardy running species that will colonize surrounding beds and lawn if left uncontained.

directions: Plant container divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil and keep evenly moist while the grove establishes. Angusta bamboo is valued for its thin-walled, narrow-leaved culms and unusual cold hardiness for a timber-sized running bamboo, tolerating winters well into zone 6. Always contain plantings with a deep rhizome barrier, since like other running Phyllostachys it spreads by underground rhizomes and can travel many feet per season in loose soil. Thin old culms periodically to keep the grove open and encourage larger new shoots.

planting.note: Install a deep rhizome barrier before planting; this is one of the most cold-hardy running bamboos available and will spread aggressively in areas without root containment.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained garden soil; this selection tolerates poor soil and wide temperature swings better than most timber-type running bamboos, making it a popular choice for northern gardeners pushing bamboo hardiness limits. Slender green culms and fine foliage give a graceful, airy grove useful for screening in colder climates. Because it runs underground like all Phyllostachys, install a sunken rhizome barrier at least 24 inches deep and check the perimeter each spring for wandering shoots.

planting.note: Clumping habit needs no root barrier, but this large tropical selection is frost-tender and reliably hardy only in the warmest parts of zone 9 and up.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light shade, watering deeply during establishment and dry spells. This striking cultivar produces bright yellow culms randomly streaked with green, one of the most widely planted ornamental bamboos throughout the tropics and subtropics. It forms a loose but non-running clump, so no rhizome barrier is required, though very large canes need ample room to arch outward as the grove matures. Protect young plantings from frost, since foliage and culms are damaged well above freezing.

planting.note: Tight non-invasive clumper needing no root barrier; give it a sheltered, frost-free site since it is one of the more cold-sensitive Bambusa species in cultivation.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in deep, fertile, well-drained soil and irrigate regularly, especially during shoot production in summer. Beechey bamboo is grown both as a large ornamental screen and for its thick, sweet-tasting edible shoots, which are harvested in the warm season. Like other Bambusa it forms a dense, well-behaved clump that never runs, so no containment barrier is needed, but plants do need generous space to accommodate the wide, sprawling base of a mature clump. It is more cold-sensitive than many timber bamboos and should be sited away from cold pockets.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops

planting.note: Non-invasive tight clumper needing no root barrier; site with afternoon shade in hot-summer climates to prevent leaf scorch.

directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil, and mulch to keep roots cool. Fargesia robusta is a stouter, faster-establishing relative of the more familiar umbrella bamboo, with thicker culms and larger leaves that give it a bolder screening presence while still forming a tight, well-behaved clump that never runs. It tolerates more sun than most Fargesia if soil moisture is adequate, but performs best with light shade in hot afternoon conditions. Because it is shade-tolerant and non-invasive, it is an excellent choice for woodland edges or narrow side-yard privacy screens.

planting.note: Non-invasive tight clumper needing no root barrier; tolerates significant shade, making it a good woodland-edge or north-side screening choice.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in cool, moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil, mulching to protect the shallow root mass from summer heat. This is one of the wild food bamboos of the giant panda in central China and shares the extreme cold hardiness typical of high-elevation Fargesia species, tolerating winters into zone 5. It forms an upright, gently arching clump that spreads slowly by short pachymorph rhizomes and never becomes invasive, so no root barrier is required. It handles considerably more shade than Phyllostachys or Bambusa species, making it well suited to understory plantings beneath high tree canopy.
sources: WWF Giant Panda Bamboo Food Plants
